newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bills rally at close, record futures traded.
newsitem.headline: NZ bills rally at close, record futures traded.

text.p: New Zealand debt markets coasted to an impressive finish on Tuesday, with the money market the star performer on the day.
Ninety-day bank bill rates ended almost 30 basis points lower after the market was caught completely off guard by surprisingly weak inflation data.
Volumes in the front futures contracts hit an all-time high, with 10,200 contracts traded. The December contract finished up 33 points at 90.99.

Bonds also rallied well in the session but lost some of their gains going into the close. The 02/00s ended at 7.63 percent, down from their 7.78 percent close on Monday. The benchmark 10-year maturity finished at 7.68 percent.

"One of the banks did a bit of selling pre-close, but it's come back bid after the close anyway. The market had quietened down, the buy had settled, and it was probably vulnerable to a bit of retracement. Combined with the sell-off in the currency it just created a bit of uncertainty," one bond dealer said.

Earlier, the Reserve Bank said September quarter underlying inflation was 0.33 percent, making 2.34 percent for the year. The bank, which aims to keep core inflation between 0-2 percent, had forecast an annual rate of 2.7 percent, and economists expected on average a 2.6 percent rise.

"It caught all the market by surprise, that number -- it's the first significant downward surprise in inflation that I can remember for a long time. It's a matter now of whether you think the numbers themselves will stack up over time," a dealer said.
Towards the close the market was also bombarded by a string of comments from New Zealand First leader Winston Peters at a press conference.

Peters, whose party holds the balance of power after Saturday's inconclusive general election, said there was an even chance of his party entering a coalition with the conservative National party, which remains as caretaker, or the main opposition Labour party.
He also commented that the currency was overvalued. The Kiwi dropped to US$0.6963/73 at the close, from 0.6989/96 shortly after the inflation data.
"The spot Kiwi reef fish obviously responded to Peters. He looks as though he's got more power than the governor of the Reserve Bank now, and the prime minister," a dealer said.

"He's been saying that for so long. It's nothing new, so I don't really know why the market reacted to it. Does that mean they think he can force whoever he coalesces with to drive the currency down? It's just illogical," he said.
"I guess what the market is looking for now is leadership from both Labour and National, to make sure it's the dog that wags the tail and not the other way around."

Credit ratings agency Standard and Poor's affirmed New Zealand's long and short term debt ratings. Dealers said there was little new in the statement but it was comforting that S&P seemed relaxed about the country's outlook.
